\section[o suspeito]{o suspeito — the suspect}

\label{lesson:PT-C295-suspeito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the detective, then the Portuguese for the clue.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o suspeito}
\textbf{o suspeito} — \textquotedblleft{}the suspect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O suspeito tem trinta anos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The suspect is thirty years old.}
\end{quote}

Also an adjective: \emph{um carro suspeito}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{suspeito} comes from Latin \emph{suspectus} \textquotedblleft{}suspected\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{suspicere} \textquotedblleft{}to look up at, to suspect\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{specere} \textquotedblleft{}to look\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o suspeito}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o suspeito}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o suspeito}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the detective, then the Portuguese for the clue, then say \emph{o suspeito} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o suspeito mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The suspect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[a suspeita]{a suspeita — the suspicion}

\label{lesson:PT-C295-suspeita}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the clue, then the Portuguese for the suspect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a suspeita}
\textbf{a suspeita} — \textquotedblleft{}the suspicion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tenho uma suspeita: foi o vizinho.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I have a suspicion: it was the neighbour.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Sob suspeita} — under suspicion.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{suspeita} goes back to Latin \emph{suspecta}, from \emph{suspicere} \textquotedblleft{}to look up at, to suspect\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[deter]{deter — to arrest, to detain; to stop}

\label{lesson:PT-C295-deter}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the suspect, then the Portuguese for the suspicion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: deter}
\textbf{deter} — \textquotedblleft{}to arrest, to detain; to stop\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A polícia deteve dois homens.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The police arrested two men.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated like \emph{ter}: \emph{detenho, deteve}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{deter} is inherited from Latin \emph{dētinēre} \textquotedblleft{}to hold back, to detain\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{tenēre} \textquotedblleft{}to hold\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deter}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deter}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{deter}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the suspect, then the Portuguese for the suspicion, then say \emph{deter} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does deter mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To arrest, to detain; to stop\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[a detenção]{a detenção — the arrest, the detention}

\label{lesson:PT-C295-detencao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the suspicion, then the Portuguese for to arrest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a detenção}
\textbf{a detenção} — \textquotedblleft{}the arrest, the detention\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A detenção aconteceu de manhã cedo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The arrest happened early in the morning.}
\end{quote}

On the news: \emph{foi feita uma detenção}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{detenção} was borrowed from Latin \emph{dētentiō} \textquotedblleft{}a holding back\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{dētinēre}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o detido]{o detido — the person arrested, the detainee}

\label{lesson:PT-C295-detido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to arrest, then the Portuguese for the arrest.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o detido}
\textbf{o detido} — \textquotedblleft{}the person arrested, the detainee\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O detido vai ser ouvido amanhã.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The man arrested will be questioned tomorrow.}
\end{quote}

The past participle of \emph{deter} used as a noun.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{detido} is the past participle of \emph{deter} \textquotedblleft{}to arrest\textquotedblright{} used as a noun; the verb comes from Latin \emph{dētinēre} \textquotedblleft{}to hold back\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
